summary: The note describes The Edsels, an American doo-wop group active in the late 1950s and early 1960s. It explains that the group was originally called The Essos, renamed to match the Ford Edsel, and that it recorded over 25 songs and appeared several times on Dick Clark's American Bandstand. It also notes that the group was unusual among doo-wop acts for signing with a major label, Capitol Records, in 1961, after earlier songs and the national hit "Rama Lama Ding Dong" helped secure the deal.
one_line: The Edsels were a late-1950s and early-1960s American doo-wop group that signed with Capitol Records in 1961 after the hit "Rama Lama Ding Dong".
key_facts: The Edsels were an American doo-wop group active during the late 1950s and early 1960s.
The group was originally named The Essos, after the oil company.
The name was changed to match the new Ford automobile, the Edsel.
The Edsels had multiple performances on Dick Clark's "American Bandstand".
The Edsels were one of the few doo-wop groups to sign with a major record label.
Most doo-wop groups of that era found success with small independent labels.
The Edsels had a national hit with "Rama Lama Ding Dong".
Songs "What Brought Us Together", "Bone Shaker Joe" and "Do You Love Me" came before the national hit.
These earlier songs helped The Edsels land a major recording contract with Capitol Records in 1961.
